newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Yorks Water squeezes H1 profits higher.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Yorks Water squeezes H1 profits higher.

text.p: British regional utility Yorkshire Water Plc said on Friday it managed to squeeze its first-half profits higher, but the results failed to stir investors.

The company, still struggling to recover from a drought last year, said its pretax profits rose to 109.4 million pounds ($184 million) in the first half from 99.5 million pounds -- within analysts' expectations of 105 to 110 million.
Yorkshire also raised its interim dividend by 12.1 percent to 10.2 pence per share, but the increase came near the low end of the 10.1 to 11.5 pence range most analysts had expected.
"Our emphasis in the first half has been on business essentials," chairman Brandon Gough told Reuters.
He added that the company was trying to restore customer confidence after it was slammed by the media and penalised by regulators for failing to handle last year's drought adequately.
Yorkshire's shares trod water after the results, rising just half a penny to 680.5 pence in midday trade.

Daniel Martin, an analyst at Barclays de Zoete Wedd, said Yorkshire's results were buoyed by the company's reduction of its infrastructure renewal charge to about 16.9 million pounds in the first half ended September 30 from 25.4 million.
"If you strip that out, the results are possibly a little bit disappointing, but only marginally so," Martin said.
To help improve its distribution system and build new projects, Yorkshire said it planned to raise its capital spending to some 380 million pounds this year from 235 million pounds in 1995/96.
The company also expected to keep capital expenditure running at about 350 million pounds per year for the next three financial years, Gough said in a telephone interview.
He added that the company aimed to find a way by the end of the financial year to reduce shareholders' funds and thus cut its overall cost of capital.
"For a utility, we have relatively too much equity, and I think that's well recognised," Gough said, adding that the company's gearing was currently at 11 percent.
The firm had yet to decide how it would cut shareholders' funds, he added.

"Until the Chancellor (of the Exchequer) threw a spanner in the works in October, probably the most logical route for a company like us would be a share buyback," he said, referring to recent British tax changes that have made buyback programmes less attractive for companies.
Yorkshire currently has shareholder approval to buy back 10 percent of its shares, which would amount to some 140 million stg based on its existing market capitalisation, he said.
"We're not promising that amount, but that is indicative of the scale of the adjustment we would make," he said.

When asked whether the company would consider paying a special dividend, Gough said, "A special dividend is a technical possibility, but it's not a route that we're particularly attracted to. Basically we are reviewing options."

Regarding Yorkshire's first-half performance, Gough said the firm's reservoirs -- which account for about half its water supply -- were currently about 75 percent full, compared to some 20 percent a year ago. The company also reduced its leakage rate to about 26 percent currently, compared to 29.5 percent a year-and-a-half ago, and aimed to lower it to 24 percent in 18 months, he said.
"(The year) 1995 was annus horribilis," Gough said.

"But in weather terms, 1996 was actually quite a challenging year. The rainfall was way below normal. So this improvement we have achieved is not on the back of a wet summer, it's on the back of a very dry summer," he added.
